opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to pattern recognition that's been built up over years and years of looking at images. An experienced radiologist has seen thousands, sometimes tens of thousands, of scans, and over time they develop this almost intuitive sense of what "normal" looks like for a given organ, a given patient population, a given imaging modality. So when something deviates from that, even subtly, it registers for them, sometimes before they can even articulate why.

What's fascinating to me is that very often they can't fully explain it. If you ask them, they might say, "The texture just looks off," or "Something about the margin of that lesion bothers me." That's a kind of tacit knowledge. It's real, it's valuable, and it's often correct, but it's very hard to write down as a set of rules.

And that's really where my interest comes in, because I think a lot of what they're perceiving is actually quantifiable information that's sitting in the image. Things like heterogeneity in the tissue, subtle differences in intensity, the shape and irregularity of a boundary. That's the premise behind radiomics: the image contains far more data than the human eye can consciously extract, and if we can measure those features computationally, we can start to capture some of what that expert is responding to, and maybe even find signals that nobody is picking up on yet.

So I don't see it as replacing that expertise. I see it as trying to understand it, make it reproducible, and put it in the hands of people who haven't had twenty years of reading scans. If a less experienced clinician, or a clinician in a place without access to a subspecialist, could have a tool that flags what that expert would have noticed, that's where I think we can make a real difference for patients.

r001.rationale: The response says experienced radiologists build pattern recognition over years of examining thousands of scans, helping them notice subtle abnormalities.

r002.rationale: It does not describe adjusting image contrast to make an otherwise unseen liver tumor visible.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a wonderful question, and honestly it's one of the things that drew me into this field in the first place. I spent years sitting in reading rooms at Memorial Sloan Kettering, and I'd watch a radiologist pull up a CT scan and, within a few seconds, point to something and say, "That doesn't look right." And I'd stare at the same image and see nothing. Just liver. Just normal-looking tissue.

What I came to understand is that what they're doing isn't really "seeing" in the way we usually think about it. It's pattern recognition built on tens of thousands of cases. They've developed an internal model of what normal looks like, with all its variation, and so when something deviates, even subtly, it pops out to them. It's a bit like how a native speaker hears a grammatical error immediately without being able to cite the rule.

But here's the part that fascinates me as a computer scientist: a lot of what they're responding to is texture. It's the heterogeneity of the tissue, the way the intensities are distributed, the edges, how a region relates to the structures around it. Those are features that a human can perceive but often can't articulate. When you ask an experienced radiologist why they flagged something, they'll frequently say, "It just looked wrong." And they're right! But that intuition is hard to teach, and it's hard to scale.

So the way I've come to think about it is that a radiologist's eye is a highly trained, somewhat opaque model. And our work in computational imaging is really about making that model explicit. Can we quantify the texture they're responding to? Can we measure the things they can't put into words? And then, interestingly, can we go beyond them? Because there's information in these images, at the pixel level, that no human eye can perceive, patterns that correlate with tumor biology, with genetics, with how a patient will respond to treatment.

I don't think of it as replacing that expertise. I think of it as trying to understand it deeply enough to extend it.

astra-6.text: I think a lot of it is pattern recognition built up over years of looking at images. An experienced radiologist may notice something very subtle—a change in texture or a distortion of normal anatomy—that someone else overlooks. They may not even be able to articulate immediately what caught their attention, but they recognize that something doesn’t look right. That expertise is remarkable, and it raises an interesting question for AI: can we learn from those patterns and help make those subtle findings easier to detect?
